title: Six of Shawwal
hook: six fasts after Ramadan are like fasting the year (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the takbirat of Eid, and your line was allahu akbar on the way. Did you say it, even under your breath, on your way somewhere? Day five hundred twelve.

The morning after Eid, the house looks like a party happened. Plates in the sink, sweets nobody can face, new clothes hung back up. For a month the whole rhythm of life was different: the pre-dawn meal, the long afternoon, the date at sunset, the night prayer. And now, suddenly, lunch is back. For some there's relief. For some, a strange little grief, as if a guest left without saying goodbye. The month after Ramadan is called Shawwal, and there's a quiet custom tucked into it: not one more month of fasting, just six more days.

The custom rests on a hadith. In Sahih Muslim, the companion Abu Ayyub al-Ansari reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that whoever fasts Ramadan and then follows it with six days of Shawwal, it is as if they had fasted for the whole span of time. Another report, from the companion Thawban, gives the arithmetic behind it. A good deed is counted ten times over, a principle the Qur'an itself states. So thirty days of Ramadan count as three hundred, and six more count as sixty. Three hundred and sixty: roughly a year. A year's fast, folded into five weeks. There are a few practical things people learn quickly. You don't fast on the day of Eid itself; the Prophet forbade fasting on the two Eids. After that, the six can be kept back to back, right after Eid, or spread through the month, a Monday here, a Thursday there. Scholars have discussed both, and many say either is fine. And people who missed days of Ramadan, through illness, travel, or for women, their monthly period, often ask which comes first, making up the missed days or the six. Here the schools give different answers, and many people simply ask a scholar they trust. Not everyone in early Islam was enthusiastic, either. Imam Malik, the scholar of Medina, is reported to have disliked making it a fixed custom, worried people might start treating it as part of Ramadan. Other schools recommend it. What the six do, for those who keep them, is keep the door from slamming shut. Ramadan ends, but the habit doesn't vanish overnight. A small part of it stays in the week.
screen: `A HADITH IN SAHIH MUSLIM.` · `THIRTY TIMES TEN, PLUS SIX TIMES TEN.` · `NOT ON EID; TOGETHER OR SPREAD OUT.` · `KEEP THE DOOR FROM SLAMMING SHUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one fast. Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture next week. Find one day that's calm enough, no big dinner, no hard workout. If you're able, and it's safe for your health, decide to fast it, from dawn to sunset. If fasting isn't possible for you, plan instead to eat one meal that day slowly, with no screen, the way a fast is broken at sunset. Write the day down somewhere you'll see it. If you pray, you can make your intention quietly now. The bell holds the time.
Shawwal. The month after Ramadan, when many Muslims keep six voluntary fasts that the hadith counts, with Ramadan, as a whole year. Today's word.
Your line: six more. Today, keep one small Ramadan habit going, the early prayer, the extra page, the shared plate, just for one more day. Day five hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Many Muslims fast six voluntary days in Shawwal, the month after Ramadan, starting after the day of Eid; some fast them consecutively and others spread them through the month.

original.note: Arabic: Shawwal, the tenth month of the Hijri year, the month after Ramadan.

trapdoor: what you thought: a few extra fasts for the very devout.
what it means: six voluntary days after Ramadan which, by the hadith's arithmetic of ten for one, round the fasting out to a year.
what a scholar hears: Sahih Muslim 1164 from Abu Ayyub; the ten-for-one arithmetic from Thawban in Ibn Majah; and the report that Imam Malik disliked fixing the custom.
